summary: RFC 4364 and RFC 4659 describe provider-provisioned Layer 3 VPNs. This document defines procedures so RSVP reservation messages can pass from one customer site to another across such a VPN, allowing admission control on the links between customer and provider edge routers.

plainLanguage.summary: A company's offices share a private network run by a carrier. This lets the offices reserve bandwidth through it end to end, not only inside the carrier's part.

questions: resource reservation across bgp mpls vpn
how does rsvp work over a bgp mpls vpn
what is the vpn-ipv4 rsvp_hop object
why can rsvp not cross an l3vpn
what is admission control on pe-ce links
subtitle: How RSVP reservations can cross a BGP/MPLS VPN so the links between customer and provider routers get admission control.

tldr.problem: A BGP/MPLS VPN hides RSVP Path messages from the egress PE router and allows customers with overlapping addresses, so RSVP cannot do admission control on the PE-CE links.
tldr.mechanism: The ingress PE sends Path messages straight to the egress PE without the Router Alert Option, using new VPN-IPv4 SESSION, SENDER_TEMPLATE, FILTER_SPEC and RSVP_HOP objects that carry a Route Distinguisher.
tldr.outcome: RSVP can reserve resources on PE-CE links, and optionally across the provider backbone using aggregate MPLS-TE tunnels. Only unicast flows are covered.

today: RFC 6016 is a Proposed Standard published in October 2010. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: The Problem with RSVP over a VPN
sections.content:
RFC 6016 builds on the BGP/MPLS VPNs of RFC 4364 (IPv4) and RFC 4659 (IPv6). Customers may run RSVP (RFC 2205) for admission control in their own networks. The links between Provider Edge (PE) and Customer Edge (CE) routers are often resource constrained, so it is useful to do admission control there too.

The RFC lists three obstacles. RSVP Path messages rely on the IP Router Alert Option, but backbone packets are MPLS encapsulated, so the egress PE may never look at the IP header. Customers can use non-unique addresses, so a PE must know which VPN a message belongs to. And a PE that receives Resv messages from other PEs must be able to tie them to the right customer VPN.

The document covers unicast flows only. Multicast is left for further study.
sections.plainLanguage: The shared network cannot tell which company's message it is looking at, because two companies may use the same house numbers. This document teaches the carrier how to sort them out.

sections.title: Model of Operation
sections.content:
The RFC traces a reservation for one point-to-point flow from a Sender behind CE1 to a Receiver behind CE2. The Sender's Path message passes CE1, then PE1, across the provider backbone to PE2, then CE2 and on to the Receiver. The Receiver's Resv message comes back the same way, using the Path state to find each previous hop (PHOP).

PE2 performs admission control on the PE2-CE2 link when the Resv arrives, and CE1 performs it on the CE1-PE1 link. The hard part is establishing Path state correctly at the PEs.

If a customer first runs RSVP only inside their sites, enabling admission control on the PE-CE links extends how much of the flow path is covered. The RFC admits that some flows may fail to reserve if a segment lacks capacity, but argues that without admission control all flows would instead suffer congestion on the bottleneck.
sections.plainLanguage: The request goes out from one office to the other, and the answer comes back along the same route. Every stop on the way checks whether there is room.

sections.title: Path and Resv Processing at the PEs
sections.content:
When PE1 gets a Path message from CE1, it finds the VRF for the incoming interface and stores the Path state in that VRF, so overlapping addresses in different VPNs never look like one session. It looks up the receiver in the VRF to find the BGP next hop, which is the egress PE. It then builds a new Path message addressed to that PE, with a VPN-IPv4 SESSION object holding the Route Distinguisher (RD) plus the IPv4 address, and a VPN-IPv4 SENDER_TEMPLATE object. The new message is sent without the Router Alert Option.

At PE2 the message is addressed to the PE itself. PE2 reads the RD and address, finds the matching VRF, stores the message, converts the objects back to plain IPv4 by dropping the RD, and sends the Path toward the receiver with the Router Alert Option.

For the Resv, PE2 matches the SESSION and FILTER_SPEC objects and the VRF to the stored Path state and performs admission control on the PE-CE link. If it succeeds, PE2 sends a Resv with VPN-IPv4 objects to PE1. If it fails, a ResvError goes toward the receiver. PE1 decodes the objects, finds the VRF and sends an ordinary IPv4 Resv to the CE; it performs no admission control in this basic case. PathError, PathTear, ResvError, ResvTear and ResvConf follow the same conversion rules.
sections.plainLanguage: The first carrier stop puts a company sticker on the request so the far stop knows whose it is. The far stop peels the sticker off and hands the request on.

sections.title: The VPN-IPv4 RSVP_HOP Object
sections.content:
PE routers, especially those separated by Option-B ASBRs, need not have direct IP reachability to each other. The new VPN-IPv4 RSVP_HOP object carries the sender's IPv4 address and Logical Interface Handle as before, plus a VPN-IPv4 address for the sender. The sender MUST advertise that address in BGP with a locally allocated label, and frames received with that label MUST be given to the local control plane.

A neighbor replying to such a message looks up the BGP advertisement and sends the RSVP message MPLS encapsulated with that label. The IPv4 address in the object is still used for neighbor matching, authentication and similar purposes.

The VPN-IPv4 address MAY be an existing address in the VRF, or one created specially. A specially created address MUST NOT be redistributed to or reachable by CEs outside the MPLS VPN, for example by using a separate "control protocols VPN". An address from one customer VRF MUST NOT signal flows in another VRF. If a PE or ASBR has no suitable address it MAY use a plain IPv4 RSVP_HOP, which is not preferred.
sections.plainLanguage: It is a return address that works inside the carrier's private network, so the reply can find its way back even when the two stops cannot reach each other directly.

sections.title: Backbone Admission Control and Inter-AS Cases
sections.content:
Core (P) routers hold no customer routes, so per-customer reservations cannot live there. For admission control across the backbone, the RFC points to RFC 4804: MPLS-TE tunnels between PEs act as virtual links of a certain capacity. When a Resv reaches the ingress PE, it checks whether enough of that capacity remains. Packets under this scheme are given a particular MPLS EXP value, and no other packets may enter the core with it unless they passed admission control.

For inter-AS operation, RFC 4364 defines Options A, B and C. In Option A each ASBR acts like a PE and the new objects MUST NOT be sent between ASBRs. In Option B the ASBR either does full RSVP admission control, or does not keep state and just forwards the Path unchanged; in that second case the VPN-IPv4 RSVP_HOP object is REQUIRED. An Option-B ASBR that gets an IPv4 RSVP_HOP and will not install state MUST NOT forward the Path and SHOULD send a PathError. Option C needs no significant change, and PE-to-PE control can use an inter-AS TE tunnel.
sections.plainLanguage: Inside the carrier's main roads, nobody tracks each company, so the carrier reserves one big lane for many companies together and hands out seats in it.

sections.title: RSVP Disabled and Other RSVP Features
sections.content:
If RSVP is not enabled on the PE-CE links, a PE SHOULD NOT discard or modify RSVP messages sent to it from a CE, nor messages destined for an attached CE. That keeps the VPN transparent for customers who run RSVP only in their own sites.

Other RSVP features need a few notes. For refresh reduction (RFC 2961), the source address of an SRefresh message MUST match the IPv4 address in the RSVP_HOP object. For cryptographic authentication (RFC 2747), that same IPv4 address identifies the security association. Aggregate RSVP sessions (RFC 3175, RFC 4860) are OPTIONAL, and are covered only where the Aggregator and Deaggregator are C/CE devices. End-to-end sessions in that case use IP protocol RSVP-E2E-IGNORE, 134, and the ingress PE treats them as ordinary customer traffic.

CE-CE RSVP-TE, which relates to RFC 5824, is left for a separate document.
sections.plainLanguage: If the carrier is not taking part, it should simply pass the customer's notes along untouched.

sections.title: New RSVP Objects
sections.content:
Section 8 defines the new objects, each with an IPv4 and an IPv6 form. The VPN-IPv4 SESSION object is Class 1, C-Type 19 (VPN-IPv6 is C-Type 20), with a 12-byte VPN-IPv4 destination address (24 bytes for IPv6), Protocol Id, Flags and DstPort. SENDER_TEMPLATE (Class 11) and FILTER_SPEC (Class 10) use C-Types 14 and 15, and the RSVP_HOP object (Class 3) uses C-Types 5 and 6. Aggregate and generic aggregate variants are also defined for aggregation.

These objects MUST NOT appear in messages sent outside the provider's backbone, except on inter-AS links in the Option-B and Option-C cases. Reserved fields MUST be set to zero on transmit and ignored on receipt.

IANA assigned the C-Types and a new error code, 37, "RSVP over MPLS Problem", with sub-code 1, "RSVP_HOP not reachable across VPN".
sections.plainLanguage: The new objects are the same forms as before, but with extra space for the company sticker.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
RSVP authentication (RFC 2747 and RFC 3097) SHOULD be supported. Because RSVP messages cross the VPN addressed directly to PE or ASBR routers without the Router Alert Option, P routers stay isolated from customer reservations.

The RFC names specific risks. A customer could send many RSVP messages to exhaust a PE's processing resources, so a PE SHOULD be able to limit the share of its resources any one CE can use. A customer could try to reserve a large part of backbone capacity, so implementations are RECOMMENDED to support local policy limiting reservations per customer or CE. Exporting PE VPN-IPv4 routes to another AS could give unchecked access to remote PEs if indiscriminately redistributed. Finally, PEs and ASBRs must accept signaling packets addressed to themselves, which a "control protocol VPN" can mitigate.

The PE-CE procedures are compatible with IPsec between PEs. The optional backbone procedures are not, since they depend on PE-PE MPLS TE tunnels.
sections.plainLanguage: Someone might flood the carrier's door with requests or hog the shared lane, so the carrier should set limits per customer.
